DragonForce Hackers Abuse Microsoft Teams Relays to Hide Backdoor.Turn C2 Traffic

The Hacker News
2026-06-18 17 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors associated with the DragonForce ransomware have been observed using a custom Go-based remote access trojan (RAT) called Backdoor.Turn to conceal command-and-control (C2) traffic inside Microsoft Teams relay infrastructure. According to findings from Broadcom-owned Symantec and Carbon Black, the backdoor was deployed against a major U.S. services firm. The name of the company was

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] PowerShell drops 'tech support hotfix' ZIP archive (DragonForce Backdoor.Turn delivery) · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — DragonForce Hackers Abuse Microsoft Teams Relays to Hide Backdoor.Turn C2 Traffi
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Bring-Your-Own-Vulnerable-Driver load (HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys + DragonForce BYOVD set) · [LLM] Backdoor.Turn injection - CreateRemoteThread / process access targeting DbgView64.exe · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Backdoor.Turn - DbgView64.exe initiating outbound network connection · [LLM] DragonForce Backdoor.Turn - Known C2 IOC contact (IP/domain/SHA256) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
PowerShell drops 'tech support hotfix' ZIP archive (DragonForce Backdoor.Turn delivery) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the initial DragonForce delivery step where a PowerShell command pulls down a ZIP archive masqueraded as a tech-support hotfix. The ZIP then stages a signed binary plus a malicious side-load DLL, so catching the drop itself prevents the side-load chain. Rationale: Article states the December 2025 intrusion began with 'a PowerShell command to drop a ZIP archive under the pretext of a tech support hotfix'. Combining PowerShell + download cmdlet + .zip + hotfix-lure keywords yields high specificity for this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/dragonforce-hackers-abuse-microsoft.html
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IT helpdesk staging real hotfix ZIPs via PowerShell scripts
  • Patch-management tooling (SCCM scripts, Intune Win32 wrappers) using PS to fetch update bundles
  • Developers downloading hotfix-named release ZIPs from GitHub via PowerShell
  • Software auto-updaters whose installer naming includes 'patch'/'update'
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe","chocolatey.exe","choco.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\WindowsApps\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract URL/host from ProcessCommandLine; resolve domain/IP against TI, sandbox the ZIP via SHA256 from DeviceFileEvents, identify the invoking user/parent (svc account vs human, scheduled task vs Outlook). 2) Contain: isolate device via Defender Live Response, block the source URL/IP at the proxy, kill PowerShell session, quarantine the dropped ZIP and any DLLs extracted from it. 3) Hunt: pivot on dropped ZIP SHA256 across the fleet, look for subsequent rundll32/regsvr32 launching DLLs out of the extracted folder (DLL side-load), scan for HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys driver writes, and review egress to known DragonForce C2 IPs (62.164.177.25, 192.36.27.51).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","DownloadFile","Start-BitsTransfer","Invoke-RestMethod","curl ","wget ")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".zip"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("hotfix","support","techsupport","patch","update","kb")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","DownloadFile","Start-BitsTransfer","Invoke-RestMethod","curl ","wget ")
| where CommandLine has ".zip"
| where CommandLine has_any ("hotfix","support","techsupport","patch","update","kb")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: PowerShell Drops Tech Support Hotfix ZIP (DragonForce Backdoor.Turn)
id: 9b1e3c8a-4a2b-4a5b-9a4a-3b8f2c1c4a01
description: Detects PowerShell downloading a ZIP archive whose name suggests a tech-support hotfix/patch lure, observed as DragonForce/Backdoor.Turn initial drop.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/dragonforce-hackers-abuse-microsoft.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  selection_download:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'Invoke-WebRequest'
      - 'iwr '
      - 'DownloadFile'
      - 'Start-BitsTransfer'
      - 'Invoke-RestMethod'
      - 'curl '
      - 'wget '
  selection_zip:
    CommandLine|contains: '.zip'
  selection_lure:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'hotfix'
      - 'support'
      - 'techsupport'
      - 'patch'
      - 'update'
  condition: all of selection_*
level: medium
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\pwsh.exe) @CommandLine:(*Invoke-WebRequest* OR *DownloadFile* OR *Start-BitsTransfer* OR *Invoke-RestMethod*) @CommandLine:*.zip* @CommandLine:(*hotfix* OR *Hotfix* OR *HOTFIX* OR *support* OR *patch* OR *update*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(invoke-webrequest|downloadfile|start-bitstransfer|invoke-restmethod|curl |wget )", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)\\.zip", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)(hotfix|support|techsupport|patch|update|kb)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") (Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadFile*" OR Processes.process="*Start-BitsTransfer*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*") (Processes.process="*.zip*" AND (Processes.process="*hotfix*" OR Processes.process="*support*" OR Processes.process="*patch*" OR Processes.process="*update*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") (Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadFile*" OR Processes.process="*Start-BitsTransfer*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*") (Processes.process="*.zip*" AND (Processes.process="*hotfix*" OR Processes.process="*support*" OR Processes.process="*patch*" OR Processes.process="*update*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
Bring-Your-Own-Vulnerable-Driver load (HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys + DragonForce BYOVD set) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for installation/load of the specific vulnerable drivers DragonForce used to silence EDR before deploying Backdoor.Turn: Huawei HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys plus wsftprm.sys (CVE-2023-52271), GameDriverX64.sys (CVE-2025-61155), K7RKScan.sys (CVE-2025-1055) and ABYSSWORKER. Filename-pivoted because the driver names themselves are the article's strongest IOC. Rationale: Article explicitly names HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys (Huawei driver) and provides the BYOVD CVE-paired set (CVE-2023-52271/wsftprm.sys, CVE-2025-61155/GameDriverX64.sys, CVE-2025-1055/K7RKScan.sys) plus ABYSSWORKER. Driver filenames are extremely rare in benign telemetry — high-fidelity pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-52271 • https://www.loldrivers.io/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068/
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001 T1014
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Huawei audio driver installation on Huawei laptops (HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys)
  • K7 Computing AV product legitimately loading K7RKScan.sys
  • WS_FTP Pro legitimate installer dropping wsftprm.sys
  • Red-team / purple-team exercises staging known LOLDrivers
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Huawei\", @"\Program Files\K7 Computing\", @"\Program Files (x86)\Ipswitch\WS_FTP\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which driver fired, capture SHA256, check if the host has a legitimate vendor match (e.g. Huawei hardware for HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys); pull the dropping process tree and registry service-create events. 2) Contain: isolate host, stop & disable the driver service, quarantine the .sys file, force a Defender scan; revoke any cached creds since BYOVD precedes credential theft in this chain. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same SHA256, look for DbgView64.exe injection events that follow within 24h (Backdoor.Turn signature), and check outbound QUIC traffic from DbgView64.exe to non-Microsoft IPs.
let BYOVDFiles = dynamic(["HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys","wsftprm.sys","GameDriverX64.sys","K7RKScan.sys","abyssworker.sys"]);
let BYOVDHashes = dynamic(["82b37a92589dfd4d67ca87eb9e52ac8e682e8e60d2211f59074cd5ccc693013b","821da79d727351dd67ce5df7950e9a3de6647a3cf474bb3a093f67507fed92a6","b6628d201c2a68d2a3de2a87de7a5acfe21b101a97928e1c8d5c82102d967383"]);
union
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
  | where FileName in~ (BYOVDFiles) or SHA256 in (BYOVDHashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="FileEvent"),
(DeviceImageLoadEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName in~ (BYOVDFiles) or SHA256 in (BYOVDHashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType="ImageLoad", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="ImageLoad"),
(DeviceRegistryEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RegistryKey has @"\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
  | where RegistryValueData has_any (BYOVDFiles)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName=RegistryValueName, FolderPath=RegistryKey, SHA256="", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="RegistryService")
| order by Timestamp desc
let BYOVDFiles = dynamic(["HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys","wsftprm.sys","GameDriverX64.sys","K7RKScan.sys","abyssworker.sys"]);
let BYOVDHashes = dynamic(["82b37a92589dfd4d67ca87eb9e52ac8e682e8e60d2211f59074cd5ccc693013b","821da79d727351dd67ce5df7950e9a3de6647a3cf474bb3a093f67507fed92a6","b6628d201c2a68d2a3de2a87de7a5acfe21b101a97928e1c8d5c82102d967383"]);
union
(ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where TargetFileName in~ (BYOVDFiles) or TargetFileSHA256 in (BYOVDHashes)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, Source="ImFileEvent"),
(ImRegistryEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where RegistryKey has @"\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
  | where RegistryValueData has_any (BYOVDFiles)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName=RegistryValueData, TargetFilePath=RegistryKey, TargetFileSHA256="", Source="ImRegistryEvent")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Backdoor.Turn injection - CreateRemoteThread / process access targeting DbgView64.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the DragonForce-specific tradecraft of injecting Backdoor.Turn into the legitimate Sysinternals DbgView64.exe process after ransomware deployment. The article calls out DbgView64.exe by name as the target host process — a very rare injection target in benign telemetry. Rationale: Article uniquely names DbgView64.exe as the legitimate Sysinternals host process Backdoor.Turn is injected into after DragonForce ransomware deploys. Sysinternals DbgView64.exe is rare in production EDR data and is almost never the target of remote-thread injection - high-precision pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/dragonforce-hackers-abuse-microsoft.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/sysinternals/downloads/debugview
ATT&CKT1055 T1055.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using Sysinternals DebugView attaching legitimately to processes for triage
  • EDR or AV product tagging DbgView64.exe with self-injection telemetry
  • Red-team C2 framework using DbgView64.exe as host process during sanctioned engagement
  • ProcExp/ProcMon performing handle enumeration that triggers OpenProcessApiCall
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Sysinternals\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("procexp64.exe","procmon64.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the injecting process (SourceImage), pull its SHA256/path and command line, confirm whether DbgView64.exe is in a non-standard folder (e.g. ProgramData, AppData) which alone is highly suspicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host via EDR live-response, dump DbgView64.exe memory for IR (look for QUIC/TURN strings), kill the process, block C2 IPs 62.164.177.25 / 192.36.27.51 at egress. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for any DbgView64.exe outbound to UDP/443, look for the BYOVD driver writes that preceded it (HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys etc.), and review prior DragonForce ransomware encryption activity within the last 60 days on the host.
// Inject-into-DbgView64.exe — CreateRemoteThread / OpenProcess on the article's named target
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("CreateRemoteThreadApiCall","OpenProcessApiCall","ProcessPrimaryTokenModified","WriteToLsassProcessMemory")
| extend TargetImage = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).TargetImage),
         TargetFileName_x = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).TargetFileName)
| where FileName =~ "DbgView64.exe" or TargetImage endswith @"\DbgView64.exe" or TargetFileName_x =~ "DbgView64.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "DbgView64.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, TargetImage, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
// Sysmon EID 8 (CreateRemoteThread) / EID 10 (ProcessAccess) targeting DbgView64.exe
WindowsEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Provider == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon"
| where EventID in (8, 10)
| extend TargetImage = tostring(EventData.TargetImage),
         SourceImage = tostring(EventData.SourceImage),
         GrantedAccess = tostring(EventData.GrantedAccess),
         CallTrace = tostring(EventData.CallTrace)
| where TargetImage endswith "\\DbgView64.exe"
| where SourceImage !endswith "\\DbgView64.exe"
| where SourceImage !endswith "\\explorer.exe" and SourceImage !endswith "\\services.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, SourceImage, TargetImage, GrantedAccess, CallTrace
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Process Injection Targeting Sysinternals DbgView64.exe (DragonForce Backdoor.Turn)
id: 8a2d4c5e-1f3b-4e5a-8b6c-2d4e6f8a1b03
description: Detects CreateRemoteThread/ProcessAccess where the target is DbgView64.exe and the source is not DbgView64 itself - the specific tradecraft used by DragonForce to host Backdoor.Turn.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/dragonforce-hackers-abuse-microsoft.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:

  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetImage|endswith: '\DbgView64.exe'
  filter_self:
    SourceImage|endswith: '\DbgView64.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_self
level: high
source:windows.sysmon (@EventID:8 OR @EventID:10) @TargetImage:(*\\DbgView64.exe OR *\\dbgview64.exe OR *\\DBGVIEW64.EXE) -@SourceImage:(*\\DbgView64.exe OR *\\dbgview64.exe) -@SourceImage:(*\\explorer.exe OR *\\services.exe)
#event_simpleName=DllInjection
| TargetImageFileName=/\\DbgView64\.exe$/i
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\\DbgView64\.exe$/i OR ContextImageFileName=/\\(explorer|services)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetImageFileName, TargetProcessId], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="DbgView64.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | where parent_process_name!="explorer.exe" AND parent_process_name!="DbgView.exe"
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="DbgView64.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | where parent_process_name!="explorer.exe" AND parent_process_name!="DbgView.exe"
Backdoor.Turn - DbgView64.exe initiating outbound network connection AICommand & Control High
Hunts DbgView64.exe — the Sysinternals tool the article confirms is hijacked as host process for Backdoor.Turn — making outbound network connections. Sysinternals DebugView is a local diagnostic tool and should never speak to the internet, especially via QUIC/UDP 443 to non-Microsoft destinations. Rationale: DebugView (DbgView64.exe) is a Sysinternals diagnostic utility that does not require network connectivity. Article confirms DragonForce uses it as host process for Backdoor.Turn QUIC C2 — any outbound from this binary is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/dragonforce-hackers-abuse-microsoft.html • https://learn.microsoft.com/sysinternals/downloads/debugview • https://www.praetorian.com/blog/ghost-calls-c2-microsoft-teams-turn/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.002 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using DebugView with network-aware sister tools — extremely rare
  • Sysinternals Live (live.sysinternals.com) update check by genuine DbgView (uses HTTPS/TCP 443 to Microsoft IP space — distinguish by destination)
  • Red-team / purple-team exercise simulating Backdoor.Turn
  • EDR/AV process tagging where DbgView64 telemetry gets attributed to a wrapper
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP startswith "13." or RemoteIP startswith "20." or RemoteIP startswith "40." or RemoteIP startswith "52.")  // exclude Microsoft AS8075 ranges (rough)
Response runbook
1) Triage: validate the destination IP/ASN (DragonForce IPs include 62.164.177.25 and 192.36.27.51; Microsoft Teams TURN egress should resolve to Microsoft AS8075). Pull file path of DbgView64.exe — anywhere outside an admin's tools folder is suspect. 2) Contain: isolate host via Defender, kill the DbgView64.exe process, block the remote IP at firewall, capture process memory before kill if forensics-ready. 3) Hunt: pivot on the remote IP across the fleet, search for any other Sysinternals binary making outbound (procexp64.exe, procmon64.exe), check for the BYOVD driver writes that preceded this connection, and review whether any DragonForce ransomware encryption activity was observed on the host in the last 90 days.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "DbgView64.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Sysmon EID 3 — network connection initiated by DbgView64.exe (parsed from EventData)
WindowsEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Provider == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 3
| extend Image = tostring(EventData.Image),
         DestIp = tostring(EventData.DestinationIp),
         DestPort = toint(EventData.DestinationPort),
         NetProtocol = tostring(EventData.Protocol),
         DestHostname = tostring(EventData.DestinationHostname)
| where Image endswith "\\DbgView64.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Image, DestIp, DestPort, NetProtocol, DestHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DragonForce Backdoor.Turn - Known C2 IOC contact (IP/domain/SHA256) AICommand & Control Medium
Pure IOC sweep on the DragonForce/Backdoor.Turn campaign indicators released in the Symantec/Carbon Black write-up: two C2 IPs, eight C2 domains, and 20 SHA256 hashes. Runs across network/DNS/file telemetry for known contact. Rationale: Pre-extracted IOC list from the Symantec/Carbon Black write-up of DragonForce Backdoor.Turn: 2 C2 IPs (62.164.177.25, 192.36.27.51), 8 C2 domains, and 20 SHA256 hashes. Pure IOC sweep across network/DNS/file telemetry — Sigma intentionally skipped because this is a multi-table union, not single-event-shape. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/dragonforce-hackers-abuse-microsoft.html • https://www.symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence • https://www.praetorian.com/blog/ghost-calls-c2-microsoft-teams-turn/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed scanner / IOC sweeper hitting these domains intentionally
  • Researcher visiting compromised-but-cleaned domain (e.g. glanz-gmbh.de after takedown)
  • Sandbox detonation of related sample inside the corporate network
  • CDN/shared-hosting collision where benign sites share an IP with a former C2 IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user that contacted the IOC, determine the initiating process and binary (look specifically for DbgView64.exe per the campaign signature), validate this isn't a TI scanner or sandbox host. 2) Contain: isolate the host via EDR, block the IPs/domains/hashes at egress proxy + DNS, quarantine any matching SHA256 files, force credential reset for the account if interactive logon occurred. 3) Hunt: timeline 60-90 days backward looking for the December 2025 entry technique (PowerShell ZIP hotfix), BYOVD driver writes (HWAuidoOs2Ec.sys), DLL side-loading, lateral movement (LDAP enumeration is a Backdoor.Turn capability), and any DragonForce ransomware staging activity.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-52271", "CVE-2025-61155", "CVE-2025-1055")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-52271", "CVE-2025-61155", "CVE-2025-1055")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2023-52271", "CVE-2025-61155", "CVE-2025-1055")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive hash match
level: critical

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Fake browser update JavaScript spawned from browser download directory (SocGholish) · [LLM] WordPress site serving injected SocGholish loader to internal browser
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Script interpreter spawning PE loader after browser-delivered JS (SocGholish second stage) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Script interpreter outbound HTTPS within 60s of Update.js execution (SocGholish) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Shadow copy deletion within 24h of SocGholish script execution (Evil Corp ransomware prelude) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Fake browser update JavaScript spawned from browser download directory (SocGholish) AIDelivery High
Detects wscript.exe/cscript.exe executing a JavaScript file named like a browser update from a user download path with a browser parent — the SocGholish/FakeUpdates execution shape described in the article. The article-specific pivots are the browser-as-parent + Update-themed JS filename. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit FakeUpdates delivery mechanism: 'tricking visitors into downloading malicious payloads, commonly disguised as fake browser updates' executed by 'JavaScript-based malware downloader'. The browser parent + .js child + Downloads/Temp + Update naming combination is what differentiates SocGholish from generic wscript usage. Cross-referenced MITRE S0760 (SocGholish) page and CISA AA22-264A on Evil Corp/FakeUpdates tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0760/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-264a
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate IT pushing self-service .js helpers via internal portals opened in Edge/Chrome
  • Browser-launched JS-based vendor installers (e.g. some Cisco WebEx legacy launchers)
  • User double-clicks legitimate .js attachment in Downloads opened with default Script Host
  • SCCM or Intune browser-driven enrollment scripts
  • Developer testing JavaScript console output through wscript locally
Suppression filter
and not InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--vendor-installer","sccm-bootstrap","intune-mam") and not FolderPath startswith @"C:\Program Files\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent browser's URL history within 10 minutes prior to the wscript launch and the SHA256 of the .js — cross-check the SHA against VirusTotal and the source URL against URLhaus/abuse.ch for SocGholish IOC overlap. 2) Contain: isolate the device via Defender Live Response or Falcon RTR, disable the user's session, kill the wscript tree, and quarantine the .js artefact. 3) Hunt: pivot on the originating URL across DeviceNetworkEvents/proxy for other users who visited the same compromised WordPress site in the last 30 days, and search DeviceProcessEvents for child processes (powershell.exe, rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe) spawned by wscript on the affected host — that's the SocGholish→Dridex/Empire/Azorult hand-off.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Update.js","Chrome_Update","Firefox_Update","BrowserUpdate","Edge_Update")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Update.js","Chrome_Update","Firefox_Update","BrowserUpdate","Edge_Update")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SocGholish Fake Browser Update Script Execution from Browser Download
id: 6c7d9b3a-2e41-4d2c-8f8a-1c2b3a4b5c6d
description: Detects wscript.exe/cscript.exe executing a JavaScript file from a user download directory with a browser as parent process - the FakeUpdates/SocGholish drive-by delivery shape.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/law-enforcement-nukes-socgholish-malware-from-nearly-15-000-sites/
  - https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0760/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
      - '\opera.exe'
  selection_path:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '\Downloads\'
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\AppData\Local\Temp\'
  selection_js:
    CommandLine|contains: '.js'
  condition: all of selection_*
falsepositives:
  - Corporate self-service scripts shipped as .js installers
  - Legitimate browser-distributed JS-based deployment tools
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) @ParentImage:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\MSEdge.exe OR *\firefox.exe OR *\Firefox.exe OR *\brave.exe) @Image:(*\wscript.exe OR *\WScript.exe OR *\WSCRIPT.EXE OR *\cscript.exe OR *\CScript.exe OR *\CSCRIPT.EXE) @CommandLine:(*.js* AND (*\Downloads\* OR *\Temp\* OR *Update.js* OR *Chrome_Update* OR *Firefox_Update* OR *BrowserUpdate*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|opera)\.exe$/i
| regex("\\.js", field=CommandLine)
| regex("\\\\(Downloads|Temp|AppData\\\\Local\\\\Temp)\\\\", field=CommandLine) OR regex("(?i)(Update\\.js|Chrome_Update|Firefox_Update|BrowserUpdate|Edge_Update)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())

Script interpreter outbound HTTPS within 60s of Update.js execution (SocGholish) AICommand & Control Medium
Correlates a wscript/cscript or post-script powershell process with an outbound HTTPS connection to a non-internal host within 60s — the SocGholish 'opens a connection to the attackers' beacon. Pivots on the temporal join, not the destination, so it survives infrastructure rotation post-Endgame takedown. Rationale: The article describes the post-execution beacon explicitly: 'the malware opens a connection to the attackers, giving them access to the infected system.' Temporal correlation between the script execution and the egress, with the parent browser as the original trigger, is what distinguishes SocGholish from benign wscript activity. The 60s window is consistent with public Mandiant / RedCanary FakeUpdates timing observations. Cross-checked against: • https://redcanary.com/threat-detection-report/threats/socgholish/ • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0760/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate JS-based installers checking license servers immediately after launch
  • Corporate browser-launched .js helpers calling internal-looking external CDN endpoints
  • Edge browser update orchestration spawning short-lived script processes
  • Self-service portal scripts polling SaaS APIs on launch
  • Vendor telemetry scripts (Citrix, Cisco) calling home post-install
Suppression filter
and not RemoteUrl has_any (".microsoft.com",".windowsupdate.com",".office.com",".live.com","login.microsoftonline.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the remote IP/URL and pivot through DeviceNetworkEvents for every host that contacted the same endpoint in the last 7 days — SocGholish C2 often fronts via compromised WordPress, so passive DNS / URLhaus lookup is the first move. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the wscript/cscript and any spawned powershell, and block the destination in proxy and EDR network policy. 3) Hunt: search for subsequent DeviceProcessEvents on the host showing wscript spawning powershell, rundll32, or PE writes to AppData — these are the Dridex/Empire/Koadic/Azorult hand-offs called out in the article.
let Window = 60s;
let Scripts = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where AccountName !endswith "$"
  | where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
  | where ProcessCommandLine has ".js"

WordPress site serving injected SocGholish loader to internal browser AIDelivery Medium
Detects internal browser HTTP/HTTPS GETs that retrieve injected JavaScript loaders matching the SocGholish profile from WordPress-hosted paths (wp-content, wp-includes, wp-admin) — the drive-by staging step described in the article. Pivots on the wp-* URL fragment + script Content-Type returning to a non-script-expecting referer. Rationale: Article's central claim is '14,971 compromised WordPress websites' delivering SocGholish via injected JS. The wp-content/wp-includes URL surface plus browser UA plus .js retrieval is the article-specific delivery shape. We avoid hardcoding domains because Operation Endgame just disinfected the known ones — the *next* compromised WP site will look identical at the URL-pattern layer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/are-you-sure-your-browser-up-date-current-landscape-fake-browser-updates • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189/
ATT&CKT1189 T1584.006
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WordPress-hosted marketing sites with JS analytics
  • Corporate blog on WordPress legitimately serving JS theme/plugin assets
  • Internal WordPress intranet sites with JS plugins
  • Cookie-consent banners loaded from wp-content
  • Third-party WordPress vendor docs sites accessed for research
Suppression filter
and not RemoteUrl has_any ("/wp-content/themes/","/wp-content/plugins/jetpack/","/wp-includes/js/jquery/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dedupe by URL+domain and run the resolved domain through URLhaus, abuse.ch ThreatFox, and the Operation Endgame seizure list — Dutch NHTCU publishes seized domains post-operation. 2) Contain: if any URL is confirmed malicious, block the FQDN at proxy/firewall and pivot to every host that visited it. 3) Hunt: for confirmed-bad URLs, search DeviceProcessEvents on the visiting host(s) for wscript/cscript children of the browser within 10 minutes — that's the executed SocGholish chain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/wp-content/","/wp-includes/","/wp-admin/admin-ajax.php","/wp-json/")
| where RemoteUrl endswith ".js" or RemoteUrl has ".js?" or RemoteUrl has "=eval"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), HostsHit = dcount(DeviceName), Hits = count() by RemoteUrl, tostring(split(RemoteUrl,"/")[2])
| where HostsHit >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("Chrome","Edg","Firefox","Brave")
| where Url has_any ("/wp-content/","/wp-includes/","/wp-admin/admin-ajax.php","/wp-json/")
| where Url endswith ".js" or Url has ".js?" or Url contains "=eval"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), HostsHit = dcount(SrcHostname), Hits = count() by Url, DstHostname
| where HostsHit >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:(zscaler OR proxy OR squid OR bluecoat) @http.url:(*\/wp-content\/* OR *\/wp-includes\/* OR *\/wp-admin\/admin-ajax.php* OR *\/wp-json\/*) @http.url:(*.js* OR *eval*) @http.useragent:(*Chrome* OR *Edg* OR *Firefox* OR *Brave*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|opera)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
| sort(count, order=asc)
| count<=2
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url LIKE "%/wp-content/%" OR Web.url LIKE "%/wp-includes/%" OR Web.url LIKE "%/wp-admin/%" OR Web.url LIKE "%/wp-json/%" by Web.src Web.user Web.url Web.url_domain Web.http_user_agent Web.http_referrer Web.http_content_type | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where like(url, "%.js%") AND (like(http_content_type, "%javascript%") OR like(http_content_type, "%text/html%")) | stats count dc(src) as host_count values(url) as urls by url_domain | where host_count >= 1
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url LIKE "%/wp-content/%" OR Web.url LIKE "%/wp-includes/%" OR Web.url LIKE "%/wp-admin/%" OR Web.url LIKE "%/wp-json/%" by Web.src Web.user Web.url Web.url_domain Web.http_user_agent Web.http_referrer Web.http_content_type | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where like(url, "%.js%") AND (like(http_content_type, "%javascript%") OR like(http_content_type, "%text/html%")) | stats count dc(src) as host_count values(url) as urls by url_domain | where host_count >= 1
Script interpreter spawning PE loader after browser-delivered JS (SocGholish second stage) AIInstallation High
Detects wscript.exe/cscript.exe spawning a PE child (rundll32, regsvr32, powershell, or a written-then-executed binary in AppData) — the SocGholish hand-off to Dridex/Empire/Koadic/Azorult/Chthonic that the article explicitly names. Filters on the wscript-parent chain so it doesn't fire on legit admin scripting. Rationale: Article calls out the loader explicitly: 'SocGholish has also been used to deploy other malware families, including Dridex, Doppelpaymer, Empire, Koadic, Chtonic, and Azorult.' That deployment universally requires wscript/cscript to spawn a follow-on process. The parent .js requirement strips legit admin scripts that don't go through a JS file. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0760/ • https://redcanary.com/threat-detection-report/threats/socgholish/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.001 T1218.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy enterprise install wrappers using cscript to drive PowerShell setup steps
  • SCCM/MECM script-based deployment phases
  • Custom internal automation: JS launcher chaining to rundll32 for COM registration
  • Adobe / Java updater chains using script host as intermediate
  • Corporate logon scripts spawning powershell for inventory
Suppression filter
and not InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","msiexec.exe","taskeng.exe") and not InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sccm-deploy","intune-package")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the spawned child's SHA256 and command line, plus the parent wscript's CommandLine — the .js path/URL gives you the originating compromised WP site. Run the binary hash through MDE/VT. 2) Contain: isolate the device, kill the wscript tree, quarantine any new PE written to AppData/Public, reset the user's session and AD creds (SocGholish loaders frequently steal Dridex-style banking creds). 3) Hunt: pivot on the JS file path/SHA across the fleet to find peers infected from the same compromised WordPress page, and run the shadow-copy-deletion UC on every confirmed host — Evil Corp commonly chains to WastedLocker/Phoenix CryptoLocker from this same chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","cmd.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wmic.exe")
   or (FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Public\") and FileName endswith ".exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          GrandparentImage = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","cmd.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wmic.exe")
   or (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Public\") and ActingProcessName endswith ".exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SocGholish Script-to-PE Hand-Off (Second Stage Loader)
id: 4b8e1f23-a712-4d50-b1a0-3c4d5e6f7a8b
description: Detects wscript.exe/cscript.exe spawning a PE loader (powershell, rundll32, regsvr32, mshta, cmd, bitsadmin, certutil, curl, wmic) - the SocGholish hand-off to second-stage payloads (Dridex, Empire, Koadic, Azorult, Chthonic).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/law-enforcement-nukes-socgholish-malware-from-nearly-15-000-sites/
  - https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0760/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1218.011
  - attack.execution
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains: '.js'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wmic.exe'
  condition: all of selection_*
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate corporate JS installers chaining to PowerShell post-install steps
  - Software-deployment helpers using cscript to drive an MSI
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) @ParentImage:(*\wscript.exe OR *\WScript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\CScript.exe) @ParentCommandLine:*.js* @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\rundll32.exe OR *\Rundll32.exe OR *\regsvr32.exe OR *\RegSvr32.exe OR *\mshta.exe OR *\MSHTA.EXE OR *\bitsadmin.exe OR *\certutil.exe OR *\CertUtil.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh|rundll32|regsvr32|mshta|bitsadmin|certutil|curl|wmic)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","cmd.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","cmd.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Shadow copy deletion within 24h of SocGholish script execution (Evil Corp ransomware prelude) AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a vssadmin/wmic/PowerShell shadow-copy deletion with a prior wscript-from-browser execution on the same host within 24h — the SocGholish→Evil Corp ransomware hand-off pattern named in the article (WastedLocker, Hades, Macaw, Phoenix CryptoLocker). This is the article's stated end-state impact. Rationale: Article explicitly attributes the chain to Evil Corp's ransomware history: 'was behind the WastedLocker, Hades, Macaw Locker, and Phoenix CryptoLocker ransomware operations.' All those families delete VSS shadow copies before encrypting; correlating that with the SocGholish script execution on the same host within 24h gives an extremely high-confidence end-stage detection. Cross-checked Mandiant's WastedLocker analysis and CISA AA22-264A which describe the exact vssadmin+bcdedit prep pattern used post-SocGholish. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-264a • https://www.mandiant.com/resources/blog/wastedlocker-ransomware-evil-corp • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0037/
ATT&CKT1490 T1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/Veritas pre-backup shadow-copy cleanup on the same host that ran a legit corporate JS deployment
  • Sysadmin manually troubleshooting VSS on a workstation that earlier ran a corporate JS installer
  • Windows Update / DISM operations clearing shadows post-cumulative update
  • ConfigMgr OS deployment task sequences calling vssadmin
  • SQL Server pre-snapshot maintenance jobs
Suppression filter
and not (VssCmd has_any ("veeam","sql","DISM","sccm","intune") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","sqlservr.exe","tiworker.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is treated as a ransomware-in-progress incident — pull the wscript .js path, the vssadmin/bcdedit cmdline, and the spawning user, and cross-check the host for file-rename storms in DeviceFileEvents during the same window. 2) Contain: isolate immediately (Defender 'Isolate device' / Falcon Network Containment), suspend the user across AD and EntraID, kill all child processes of wscript, and block the originating compromised WP domain at proxy/firewall. Alert IR leadership and engage Evil Corp playbook (WastedLocker/Phoenix CryptoLocker). 3) Hunt: pivot on the user/host across the fleet for lateral movement (SMB writes, WMI exec, PsExec) in the prior 6h; look for the originating compromised WordPress URL in proxy logs across the org and quarantine every host that visited it.
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let Scripts = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where AccountName !endswith "$"
  | where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
  | where ProcessCommandLine has ".js"
  | project ScriptTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, ScriptCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Win32_Shadowcopy","Remove-WmiObject Win32_Shadowcopy","Get-WmiObject Win32_Shadowcopy"))
   or (FileName =~ "bcdedit.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("recoveryenabled no","bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures"))
| join kind=inner Scripts on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (ScriptTime .. ScriptTime + LookbackHours)
| project ScriptTime, VssTime = Timestamp,
          DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, ScriptTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, ScriptCmd,
          VssBinary = FileName, VssCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by VssTime desc
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let Scripts = ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
  | where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
  | where ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has ".js"
  | project ScriptTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ScriptCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "vssadmin.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
   or (ActingProcessName has "wmic.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
   or (ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Win32_Shadowcopy","Remove-WmiObject Win32_Shadowcopy"))
   or (ActingProcessName has "bcdedit.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("recoveryenabled no","bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures"))
| join kind=inner Scripts on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (ScriptTime .. ScriptTime + LookbackHours)
| project ScriptTime, VssTime = TimeGenerated,
          DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, ScriptTime),
          DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ScriptCmd,
          VssBinary = ActingProcessName, VssCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by VssTime desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) ((@Image:(*\vssadmin.exe OR *\VSSAdmin.exe OR *\VSSADMIN.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*delete* AND *shadows*)) OR (@Image:(*\wmic.exe OR *\WMIC.exe) AND @CommandLine:(*shadowcopy* AND *delete*)) OR (@Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe) AND @CommandLine:(*Win32_Shadowcopy* OR *Remove-WmiObject*Shadowcopy*)) OR (@Image:(*\bcdedit.exe OR *\BCDEdit.exe) AND @CommandLine:(*recoveryenabled?no* OR *bootstatuspolicy?ignoreallfailures*)))

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Cotonti CVE-2026-55742 CSRF Exploit Against admin.rights.php AIExploitation Medium
Detects HTTP requests against the Cotonti admin rights handler (system/admin/admin.rights.php) carrying the vulnerable a=update action with a Referer header that does not originate from the same host. Because the vulnerable code path skips cot_check_xg() the cross-origin Referer is the most reliable wire-level indicator that the request was forged rather than initiated from inside the admin UI. Rationale: Pulls the article's exact vulnerable path (system/admin/admin.rights.php) and the vulnerable action token (a=update from cot_auth_add_group / the rights-update branch that skips cot_check_xg). The Referer-origin check is the reliable CSRF wire-fingerprint: a legit admin click comes from the same host, a forged-from-attacker-page click does not. No external corroboration sources searched — single GHSA advisory only.
ATT&CKT1190 T1068 T1546
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin who navigated to admin.rights.php directly from a bookmark or typed URL (empty Referer)
  • Site relaunch redirects where Referer header is stripped by an intermediary proxy / WAF
  • Internal QA / synthetic monitoring that exercises the admin panel from an external monitoring host
  • Browser plugins (privacy extensions) that strip the Referer header on intra-site navigation
  • Reverse-proxy fronting Cotonti where Referer points at the proxy FQDN while Computer is the backend hostname
Suppression filter
// Sentinel refinement — exclude same-origin admin panel use
| where not(csReferer matches regex strcat(@"(?i)^https?://", tostring(Computer), @"([:/].*)?$"))
| where csUserAgent !contains "SyntheticMonitor" and csUserAgent !contains "Pingdom"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full request (csUriStem + csUriQuery + csReferer + cIP), identify the admin account in csUserName, and confirm whether the Referer host is owned by your org or by an external party. If external, treat as confirmed exploit attempt. Step 2 — Contain: invalidate the admin's session cookies, force a password reset, and audit the cotonti groups table for newly created or rights-elevated groups (especially anything granted admin-equivalent rights since the alert window). Step 3 — Hunt: review the same host for follow-on template / configuration writes by the admin user (since Cotonti admins can edit templates → RCE), look for any file_writes under the Cotonti install path, and pivot on cIP to find other affected admins or other Cotonti instances targeted by the same campaign.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has "admin.rights.php" or RemoteUrl has_all ("admin.rights.php", "a=update")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          Browser = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          BrowserCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has "admin.rights.php"
| where csUriQuery has "a=update"
| where scStatus between (200 .. 399)
| extend SameOrigin = iff(csReferer matches regex strcat(@"(?i)^https?://", tostring(Computer), @"([:/].*)?$"), true, false)
| where SameOrigin == false or isempty(csReferer) or csReferer == "-"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csUserName, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csReferer, csUserAgent, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra npm Supply Chain Attack: 140+ Packages Backdoored via easy-day-js Typosquat

StepSecurity
2026-06-18 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On June 17, 2026, an attacker compromised the @mastra npm organization and quietly added easy-day-js as a dependency across 140+ packages in the Mastra AI framework ecosystem. easy-day-js is a typosquat of the popular dayjs date library, and its latest version contained an obfuscated postinstall dropper that downloaded and ran a second-stage payload from attacker-controlled servers, then deleted itself to remove any trace. Packages with a combined weekly download count exceeding 1.1 million were exposed. If you installed any @mastra package today, treat your environment as compromised.

ATT&CKT1027 T1190 T1195.002
IPs23.254.164.92 23.254.164.123

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] easy-day-js typosquat installed in node_modules (setup.cjs + package.json drop)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Mastra npm Supply Chain Attack: 140+ Packages Backdoored via easy-day-js Typosqu
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Node.js postinstall executing setup.cjs --no-warnings (easy-day-js dropper)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Mastra supply-chain C2 traffic to 23.254.164.92 / 23.254.164.123 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] easy-day-js dropper writes .pkg_history / .pkg_logs beacon files in temp · [LLM] easy-day-js dropper self-deletes setup.cjs from node_modules (forensic evasion)
Mastra supply-chain C2 traffic to 23.254.164.92 / 23.254.164.123 AICommand & Control High
Detects developer workstations, CI runners, or AI-service hosts contacting the easy-day-js stage-1 download server (23.254.164.92:8000) or stage-2 C2/exfil endpoint (23.254.164.123:443). Both IPs are dedicated to this campaign with no legitimate use. Rationale: Article explicitly names 23.254.164.92:8000 as the stage-1 download host and 23.254.164.123:443 as the stage-2 C2 / exfil endpoint passed as argv[2] to the spawned Node process. Both IPs are unique to this campaign per the StepSecurity blog and the campaign's threatfox-style block-listing. Hits should be treated as confirmed compromise pending payload triage.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • StepSecurity Harden Runner block-list lookup test traffic from security tooling
  • Threat-hunter / IOC-rotation scripts beaconing to detonate the IPs from a sandbox
  • Honeypot / canary tokens deliberately pointing at the IOCs
  • Pen-test team replaying the dropper for awareness exercises
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("harden-runner.exe","step-security-agent.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents on the alerting host for the last 14d — confirm node.exe spawned setup.cjs from a node_modules\easy-day-js path; capture the parent npm context. 2) Contain: isolate the host in MDE / EDR, kill the node process tree, and immediately rotate every secret that was readable from process.env on that host — ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/SECRET, GITHUB_TOKEN, NPM_TOKEN, GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, database secrets. 3) Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessAccountName to find other hosts logged in as the same user; query DNS + proxy for 23.254.164.0/24; audit CI runners that built any repo with @mastra in package.json since 2026-06-17 01:01 UTC; check npm + GitHub audit logs for token-use anomalies in the 24h after the install.
